_comment: Substances whose natural dose input is a concentration applied to a measured volume rather than a mass typed directly. Alcohol (percent_by_volume: grams = volume x strength/100 x density) and injectable estradiol esters (mass_per_volume: mg = volume x concentration in mg/mL, no density term) are the adopters. What belongs here is the exact conversion inputs, never a model or a threshold. Estradiol ships NO concentration preset: a vial's mg/mL varies by ester and product, so the user enters it (and saves their own presets) — 'volume is meaningless without concentration' (transfemscience.org).

substances.notes: Injectable estradiol esters are drawn from an oil vial in millilitres; the dose in mg is volume x the vial's concentration (mg/mL). The concentration is user-entered because it varies by ester and product (e.g. estradiol valerate 20-40 mg/mL, cypionate 5 mg/mL) — no shipped default. Only surfaced on IM/SC routes; oral/transdermal estradiol stays a plain mg log.

substances.standardUnitSource: NIAAA, What Is A Standard Drink?; https://www.niaaa.nih.gov/alcohols-effects-health/overview-alcohol-consumption/what-standard-drink
substances.notes: Density is the reference-table value for anhydrous ethanol at 20 C (CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, Physical Constants of Organic Compounds; the OIML R 22 international alcoholometric tables the %ABV convention itself rests on agree). It carries no citation id because a physical constant from a reference table has no paper behind it, and temperature variance across drinking temperatures is far below the precision of a poured volume. The US standard drink is a comparison gloss for reading a logged amount, not a threshold — the same pour is 1.75 units in the UK (8 g) and 1.4 in Australia (10 g).
